children.text: A Spanish fort in northern Palawan, first raised as a wooden stockade by Recollect missionaries in 1667 and rebuilt in coral stone in the 18th century. It stands on a rock jutting into Taytay Bay, so its walls look out over the calm bay and its islands.

Fort Santa Isabel stands on a rock jutting into Taytay Bay in the heart of Taytay, a small town on the east coast of northern Palawan. Its Spanish name is Fuerza de Santa Isabel, and locals usually call it "Taytay Fort." It sits on the national highway between Puerto Princesa and El Nido, making it an easy stop for travelers crossing northern Palawan, and it is one of the few places in a province known for white beaches and limestone islands where you can see Spanish colonial walls still intact.
Its history goes back to

. Augustinian Recollect missionaries first put up a wooden stockade to guard against raids by Muslim seafarers coming up from the southern seas, and the marker installed by the National Historical Commission (NHCP) in
also gives this year as the fort's beginning. Some researchers believe a stockade already existed in the
, in the early years of the mission. When the stockade decayed, rebuilding in stone began in the
, and by around
the fort had taken the basic form you see today. The name "Santa Isabel" is said to have been given in the 19th century in honor of Queen Isabella II of Spain.
Founded around
, Taytay is one of the oldest Spanish settlements in Palawan. In
it was the capital of Calamianes province, which covered all of Palawan, and from

it was the capital of Castilla province, which governed northern Palawan. The fort was the base from which Spain ruled Palawan, then called Paragua. Its plan is an irregular quadrilateral that follows the shape of the rock, with a bastion at each of the four corners; according to old records, the two seaward bastions are rounded and the two landward ones are angular. The walls were built of cut coral limestone, and a small chapel stands on the high ground inside.
In

, the Taytay municipal government, with help from the National Historical Commission, began restoring the fort, starting with the chapel, under its "Estrella del Norte" (Star of the North) heritage project. Today it looks like a small park with a lawn, flowering trees, and a small exhibit room. It is compact enough to see in
30 minutes–1 hour

, so it suits travelers interested in history and anyone looking for a break on the way to El Nido or San Vicente. If you came to Palawan only for the beaches, it makes a short pause that shows you another side of the island.

blocks.title: Main gate and coat of arms

children.text: Above the landward main gate, a crowned Spanish royal coat of arms and a three-panel relief of saints and the Virgin and Child are carved in stone, with a "Fuerza de Sta. Isabel 1667" sign hanging below. Inside the gate, stone steps lead up to the courtyard on top of the rock. The texture of the moss-covered coral stone shows best in the morning when the sun is low.

blocks.title: Walk the walls and see the stone watchtower

children.text: Climb the steps and walk around the courtyard on top of the walls to see the corner bastions and a small stone watchtower. Looking out at the sea through the tower's narrow openings, you can imagine how soldiers once watched ships entering the bay. Some edges of the walls have low railings, so take care.

blocks.title: Old cannons aimed at the sea

children.text: Old cannons on wooden-wheeled carriages are placed around the courtyard, pointing out to sea. With the calm bay and the islands beyond lined up behind the barrels, this is the fort's most popular photo angle. Do not climb on or hang from the cannons; take your pictures from the side.

On the upper part of the courtyard is a small chapel with coral-stone walls and an arched doorway. Inside are a simple altar, a wooden cross, and long pews, and it was the first part repaired during the
restoration project. It is still a place of prayer, so take off your hat and look around quietly.

One room inside the fort has information boards on the history of the fort and of Taytay. Read about the Recollect missions, the years as capital of Calamianes province, and how the wooden stockade became a stone fort before you walk the walls, and the same stones will look quite different.

The fort faces Taytay Bay to the east, so from the walls you see the calm bay, the ridges on the far shore, and islands large and small. Because the sun rises over the bay, the walls and the sea are at their most beautiful in the morning light, and at low tide the rocks and seabed below the fort are exposed.

Leaving the fort and walking down to the beach beside it, you see the whole wall standing on its rock beyond the bangka fishing boats, and from the hill above town the fort, the bay, and the village fit into one frame. Most of the best-known photos are taken from these two angles.
Near the fort are the Santa Monica Church built by the Recollects, the town plaza, and the morning market. The Taytay parish, begun in the
, is counted among the oldest parishes in Palawan. An hour's walk combined with the fort gives you a feel for this small town that was once a provincial capital.

children.text: Browse the town market and bakeries and have a light breakfast of pandesal and coffee.
Enter the fort at opening time, pay the entrance fee, and look at the coat of arms and reliefs above the gate.
Climb the stone steps and walk the courtyard on the walls, seeing the bastions, the stone watchtower, and the cannons in turn.
Visit the chapel and the exhibit room and read about the history of the fort and Taytay.
Photograph Taytay Bay and its islands in the morning light from the walls.
Walk down to the beach beside the fort and take in the whole fort beyond the bangka boats. At low tide you can walk close to the rocks.
Stroll around Santa Monica Church and the plaza.
Finish with a lunch of grilled fish and kinilaw at a restaurant in town.

items.title: Stop on the way
items.subtitle: On the road from Puerto Princesa to El Nido

children.text: Take the first shared van from Puerto Princesa to Taytay. Confirm the departure point when you book.
Arrive in Taytay town and go to the fort by tricycle or on foot.
See the main gate, walls, chapel, and exhibit room, and look out over the bay from the walls.
Have a seafood lunch at a restaurant in town and check the times of vehicles bound for El Nido.
Head to El Nido. The drive takes about
1–1.5 hours
, so you reach El Nido before dark.

Shared vans from Taytay to El Nido are not frequent, so check the next departure as soon as you arrive in town. If there are three or more of you, it is easier to hire a vehicle in Puerto Princesa or El Nido and plan a one-hour stop at the fort, with no worries about luggage.
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly daily from Manila to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS), taking about
1 hour 20 minutes
. One-way fares are about
depending on the season, and there are also direct flights from Cebu and Clark.
El Nido Airport (ENI) is closer, about
60 km
north of the fort, but since
March 29, 2026
there have been no direct flights from Manila, so it is served only from Clark, Cebu, and a few other cities. If you fly into El Nido, coming down by road is faster.
Shared vans from Puerto Princesa to Taytay take about
4–4.5 hours
and cost about
one way. A fuel surcharge may be added.
Depending on the operator, there are several departures from
to
, and return vans leave Taytay from
until late afternoon. Departure points such as San Jose Terminal vary by operator, so confirm when you book.

Most vans drop passengers at the town terminal in Taytay, but some operators go on to Liminangcong port on the west coast. Tell the driver in advance that you want to get off in Poblacion, where the fort is.
Taytay is about
60 km
south of El Nido by road, about
1–1.5 hours

by car. Some vans and buses between El Nido and Puerto Princesa pass through Taytay, so you can get off on the way, but fares and whether drop-offs are allowed vary by operator, so check when you book.

For a day trip from El Nido, hiring a vehicle or renting a motorbike gives you the most freedom. The national highway is mostly paved, but stretches under construction can turn muddy in the rainy season.
Taytay is about
50 km
by road from San Vicente Long Beach and about
90 km
from Port Barton. Direct public transport from either place is rare, so hire a vehicle or change to a van on the Puerto Princesa–El Nido route.
The fort is in the middle of Poblacion, so you can walk there from accommodation in town. From the van terminal it is a short tricycle ride; agree on the fare before you get on.
Northern Palawan, including Taytay, has a dry season from
December to May
and a rainy season from
June to November
. The fort is outdoors with little shade, so the dry season is best, and
December–February
is especially comfortable for walking the walls because mornings and evenings are relatively cool.
March–May
brings calm seas and clear skies for good photos, but midday temperatures reach around
, so go at opening time.

In the rainy season the southwest monsoon (habagat) brings frequent showers, stretches of the highway under construction can turn muddy, and vans may run late. Northern Palawan is hit directly by typhoons less often than the central Philippines, but as Typhoon Tino's landfall in neighboring El Nido in
November 2025
showed, typhoons can pass through in
October–December
as well, so check the forecast before you set out.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Taytay town (Poblacion) has pensions, guesthouses, and a few small boutique hotels. Pensions cost about
a night and mid-range hotels around

, and on the islands of Taytay Bay there are upscale island resorts reached by boat. Lodging is scarcer and simpler than in El Nido, but the town is that much quieter. Most travelers stop at the fort on the way to El Nido or San Vicente, so you can easily fit it into a travel day without staying overnight.

Taytay lies between Taytay Bay to the east and, to the west, Malampaya Sound, counted among Palawan's richest fishing grounds, so fish, squid, crab, and other seafood are plentiful. Local restaurants serve grilled fish, kinilaw (raw fish dressed in vinegar), and sinigang, a sour soup, at modest prices, and in the morning the pandesal from bakeries around the market is a treat. Palawan cashew nuts make good souvenirs. Take care of meals and water in town before or after your visit to the fort.
Opening hours are generally said to be around
, but some visitors have found the fort closed. Go in by
at the latest.
The fort faces the bay to the east, so mornings are best for photos. The sun sets behind the hills beyond town, so expect a soft evening glow rather than a sunset over the sea.
Have the roughly
entrance fee ready in small bills. In a small town like this, cash is easier than cards.
There is little shade on the walls, so a hat, sunscreen, and water are essential.
The stone steps are steep and slippery after rain, so wear shoes with firm soles.

If you are traveling between El Nido and Puerto Princesa, ask the van operator in advance about getting off in Taytay and the next departure, and if you are in a group, hire a vehicle and build a one-hour stop at the fort into your plan.
Read the boards in the exhibit room before you walk the walls, and the change from wooden stockade to stone fort will be much easier to see.
The chapel is a place of prayer, so keep quiet and avoid revealing clothing.
At low tide, walk down to the beach beside the fort to photograph the fort on its rock from below. The water comes in at high tide, so check the tide times.
Even after the restoration project that began in

, parts of the fort or the whole site may close temporarily for repairs or events, and some visitors have reported finding it closed. If you are making a long trip specifically to see it, check the latest notices through your accommodation or the Taytay municipal tourism office.
Some edges of the walls and bastions have low railings or none at all. Keep hold of children's hands and stay away from the edges.
Stones on the old watchtower and bastions are loose in places, so do not climb them, and stay out of areas marked as restricted.
The walls get very hot at midday. Watch out for dehydration and heatstroke, and drink water often.
In the rainy season and during typhoons, vans on the highway may run late or stop running. The last vans leave Taytay around
4–6 PM
, so allow plenty of time if you need to move on the same day.
The beach and rocks have sharp shells and slippery moss. Wear sandals when walking at low tide.
